flawed_step: Lines 0031 and 0035 (and the concluding sentence of 0037): the claim that the RR row has "exactly the same cost under the two strategies", hence "dispatch-A is not better under any scenario", hence dispatch-closest is "globally optimal". The L/R bucketing of line 0019 replaces each incident by its bucket-average (0.25 / 0.75), which destroys the within-bucket dependence on the actual position t1. Once t1 is kept as a real number, dispatch-A is strictly better for a whole range of first-incident positions, and the closest-ambulance rule is not optimal.
counterexample:
Use the proof's own model: A and B at 0, C at 1, incidents i.i.d. uniform on [0,1], cost = distance, two incidents, dispatched ambulances never return. Take the first incident at t1 = 0.6 (so C is genuinely closer: 0.4 vs 0.6).

(a) Dispatch closest (send C): immediate cost 1 - 0.6 = 0.4. Remaining fleet is A and B, BOTH at 0, so the second incident costs t2, with E[t2] = 0.5. Conditional expected total = 0.4 + 0.5 = 0.90.

(b) Dispatch A (the strategy the proof claims is never better): immediate cost 0.6. Remaining fleet is B at 0 and C at 1, so the second incident costs min(t2, 1-t2), with E = 0.25. Conditional expected total = 0.6 + 0.25 = 0.85.

0.85 < 0.90, so at t1 = 0.6 sending the farther ambulance is strictly better in expectation. In general, sending A instead of C at position t1 costs 2*t1 - 1 extra now and saves 0.5 - 0.25 = 0.25 later, so it wins for every t1 in (0.5, 0.625).

This is not a measure-zero curiosity: the threshold policy "send C only if t1 > 0.625" has expected two-incident total
  C(0.625) = 0.625^2/2 + 0.25*0.625 + 0.375^2/2 + 0.5*0.375 = 0.1953125 + 0.15625 + 0.0703125 + 0.1875 = 0.609375,
versus the nearest-ambulance policy (threshold 0.5): C(0.5) = 0.125 + 0.125 + 0.125 + 0.25 = 0.625. So 0.609375 < 0.625 and dispatch-closest is beaten by a strictly better policy in exactly the model the proof sets up.

Also, line 0031's pointwise claim fails outright: with t1 = 0.6, t2 = 0.9 (an RR outcome), dispatch-closest costs (1 - 0.6) + 0.9 = 1.3 while dispatch-A costs 0.6 + (1 - 0.9) = 0.7. The RR row is equal only after averaging over the whole right half, not "exactly the same cost".
reasoning_summary: The proof's narrow comparison (always-closest vs always-send-A-first) does come out in favor of always-closest: 0.625 vs 0.75 expected total over two incidents. But the proof overreaches to "dispatch-closest is globally optimal", and the argument used to get there is invalid. By collapsing each incident into an L/R bucket with fixed average trip lengths 0.25 and 0.75, the payoff table hides the fact that the immediate penalty for sending the far ambulance, 2*t1 - 1, varies continuously inside the R bucket while the future benefit is a constant 0.25. Whenever t1 lies in (0.5, 0.625) the future benefit exceeds the immediate penalty and sending A beats sending C; at t1 = 0.6 the conditional expected totals are 0.85 (send A) versus 0.90 (send C). The optimal threshold policy is therefore "send C only when t1 > 0.625", with expected cost 0.609375, strictly below the nearest-ambulance policy's 0.625. Line 0031's assertion that the RR row has exactly the same cost under both strategies is likewise false pointwise (t1 = 0.6, t2 = 0.9 gives 1.3 vs 0.7); it holds only in bucket-average, which is the very conflation of pointwise equality with expected equality that makes the optimality conclusion unjustified. The OP's intuition that it can pay to preserve fleet spread is in fact correct in this model, contrary to the proof's headline claim.
